transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Lee, I’m here because... honestly, for over a year now I’ve been trying to get someone to actually take this seriously. It started with the new ticket rotation and these security audits at work. Management keeps showing me the system logs and telling me it’s just standard company policy, but it's obvious they’re being used to build a paper trail against me. 

It's like... well, it actually reminds me a lot of back in '98 when we were migrating the old servers. I was the only one on the floor who really understood the legacy architecture we had running. My manager back then, Tom, he ended up retiring and moving out to Arizona. Bought a house right near a golf course, even though the guy didn't even golf. I never understood the appeal of the desert, honestly. It's just too dry. My sinuses can't handle a climate like that, I need a little humidity. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the audits. Yeah, they just keep pointing to the logs and saying it's policy, but I know they're tracking me specifically to push me out.
Over this past year, have you noticed any periods where your mood was unusually high, energetic, or irritable, or alternatively times when you felt very depressed or lost interest in things?

No, I haven't had anything like that. My mood is... well, it's just normal. I mean, I get a little tired sometimes, but that's just what happens when you hit 60. I actually started drinking this new French roast coffee to help with my energy in the mornings. My daughter sent it to me for my birthday. She moved up to Seattle a few years ago—you know, the coffee capital of the world. 

It rains constantly up there, though. I went to visit her last fall and I swear we didn't see the sun for six days straight. We went down to that market, the one where they throw the fish over the counter? Pike Place, I think. Honestly, watching them toss those giant salmon right over the crowd... all I could think about was the liability. Someone slips on a wet floor or gets hit in the head with a twenty-pound fish, and you're looking at a massive lawsuit. We had a guy in the IT department once, Jerry, who slipped on a spilled soda in the server room and was out on worker's comp for three months. Total nightmare for the scheduling rotation. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my mood. Yeah, no, I'm not depressed or bouncing off the walls or anything. I'm just stressed because of what management is doing to my system logs.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to hear or see?

No, nothing like that. I don't hear things or see things. My hearing is actually still pretty sharp for my age, which is lucky because my dad lost his hearing in his left ear when he was only 50. He worked in a manufacturing plant, stamping metal parts for old Ford trucks. The noise in those places was just unbelievable, no safety regulations back then, no ear protection. 

He had this old Chevy pickup himself, actually. Two-tone, blue and white. We used to drive it down to the lake on weekends and try to catch bass. I never had much patience for fishing, though. You just sit there staring at the water for hours. I always preferred tinkering with the radio in the truck, trying to get a clear signal from the station out in the city. I think that's where I first got interested in electronics and systems, just trying to figure out how all those wires connected to pull music out of thin air. 

But no... I don't hear voices or anything. Just the normal sounds of the office. And the clicking of my keyboard when I'm checking those logs they keep messing with.
Do you have any medical conditions—such as thyroid problems, seizures, head injuries, or use of alcohol or drugs—that started around the same time these concerns about being tracked began?

No, I don't have any of that. No thyroid issues, no head injuries... I don't really drink much either, maybe a beer at a barbecue, but that's about it. I did hit my head once, though, back when I was a teenager. I was riding my bike down this steep hill near our house. It was a Schwinn, one of those classic ten-speeds, bright red. I saved up all summer working at a hardware store just to buy it. 

The owner of that store, Mr. Henderson, he was a real stickler for organizing the inventory. He made me count every single box of nails and screws by hand. Took me three days just to do the plumbing aisle. But I guess it taught me a lot about keeping things categorized, which is probably why I ended up in IT. You know, making sure all the data is in the right place, everything sorted. It's funny how things you do when you're 15 end up shaping your whole career. 

Anyway, I was flying down that hill on the Schwinn, hit a patch of gravel, and went right over the handlebars. Cracked my helmet right down the middle, but the doctor said I was fine, just a mild concussion. That was over forty years ago, though. 

But what were you asking? Oh, right, medical stuff recently. No, nothing like that. My health is fine. It's just the stress from work, with them manipulating the system to build this case against me.
Aside from the stress this is causing you, has your ability to do your job, get along with coworkers, or manage your day-to-day life changed at all over this past year?

Well, my day-to-day life is fine, mostly. I mean, I still get up, make my coffee—that French roast I mentioned—and get to the office on time. But work... work has definitely gotten more difficult. I've started avoiding certain network projects lately. I just don't want them having more access to my activity than they already do. And I find myself writing these really long, defensive notes in all my support tickets now, just to have a paper trail, you know? To prove I did exactly what I was supposed to do. 

It’s funny how much paperwork has changed, actually. When I first started in IT back in the late 80s, we used these triplicate carbon-copy forms for support requests. You had to press down so hard with your pen just to make sure the yellow and pink sheets got the ink. My hand used to cramp up by the end of the week. I had this one pen, a silver Parker Jotter, that my grandfather gave me when I graduated college. He was a surveyor, always out in the field mapping property lines. He used to say a good pen was as important as a good compass. I lost that pen during a move about ten years ago. It fell behind a heavy oak bookshelf and I just never bothered to pull the shelf out to get it. 

But anyway, yeah, the ticket notes. It takes up a lot of my time now. And the team meetings have gotten really tense. I guess I'm slowing down collaboration because I'm double-checking everything they ask me to do. It's just hard to work with people when you know management is using them to monitor you.
Aside from what's happening at work, do you feel that other people outside of work—like neighbors, family members, or strangers—are also watching, tracking, or trying to harm you in some way?

No, no... outside of work, everything is pretty normal. It's really just the management at the office and the people they've got keeping tabs on me there. My neighbors are fine. Well, actually, the guy next door, Frank, he just bought this massive riding lawnmower. It's one of those zero-turn ones, bright orange, looks like a small tractor. He spends half of his Saturday just driving it around his yard, which isn't even that big, to be honest. 

I used to mow my own lawn with a push mower, an old Toro. Had it for probably fifteen years. You really had to put your back into it, especially when the grass got thick after a rainy week. My wife—before she passed—used to plant these beautiful hydrangeas along the fence line, and I always had to be so careful not to clip them when I was turning the mower around. She had this whole system for getting the soil pH just right so the flowers would turn that deep, vibrant blue instead of pink. She used to save coffee grounds and eggshells in this little ceramic compost bin on the kitchen counter. It drove me crazy sometimes, the smell of it, but she loved those flowers. 

But no, Frank's a good guy. He's not watching me or anything, just obsessed with his lawn. And my sister calls on Sundays, same as always. It's strictly a work thing. They're just trying to push me out before my pension fully vests, I know it. But nobody outside the company is involved in that.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, systematized persecutory delusion (belief that management is tracking him and building a case to force him out) lasting over one year. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech or behavior indicative of a broader psychotic process, and mood symptoms (mania/depression) are explicitly denied. Functioning is relatively preserved outside the delusional belief system—he continues working, maintains relationships with family and neighbors, and daily self-care is intact—though the delusion causes circumscribed occupational impairment (avoidance of projects, defensive documentation, strained team interactions). Medical/substance causes and head injury are ruled out as temporally unrelated. The tangential, over-inclusive speech reflects circumstantiality rather than formal thought disorder. This clinical picture—non-bizarre, encapsulated persecutory delusion of >1 month duration without hallucinations, mood episodes, or broader functional decline—is most consistent with Delusional Disorder, persecutory type (F22), rather than Schizophrenia (which requires additional psychotic features/functional deterioration) or a mood disorder with psychotic features (denied mood symptoms).
